title: Trump: ICE uses online blacklist to target anti-war student protestors

prior_terminal_row.title: Trump: ICE uses online blacklist to target anti-war student protestors
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Trump: ICE uses online blacklist to target anti-war student protestors
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: A supplied summary of July court testimony by DHS official Peter Hatch says analysts formed a “Tiger Team” to review student protesters, used Canary Mission and another list, and prepared reports on more than 5,000 people. The account says information moved through Homeland Security Investigations to the State Department for possible removal decisions; final enforcement outcomes are not supplied.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: A supplied summary of July court testimony by senior Department of Homeland Security official Peter Hatch describes analysts forming a “Tiger Team” to review student protesters. According to that account, the team used names from Canary Mission and another list and produced reports on more than 5,000 people. Information went through Homeland Security Investigations, which sent material to the State Department for possible removal decisions, according to the supplied account. Hatch reportedly said he had received verbal direction to consult Canary Mission, though he did not consider it an authoritative source; the summary also says speech such as “free Palestine” was among the phrases discussed. The account raises questions about how online material and political expression entered immigration review. It does not establish that every person named faced enforcement, that anyone was removed, or that the online list itself determined a case. The linked timeline summarizes testimony but does not include the transcript, formal unit order, full list of people reviewed or records of resulting decisions. Those documents are needed to establish the unit’s mandate, the scale of its work and what consequences followed.

title: Crypto Pardon Economy: Executives Buy Clemency Through Trump Ties

prior_terminal_row.title: Crypto Pardon Economy: Executives Buy Clemency Through Trump Ties
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Crypto Pardon Economy: Executives Buy Clemency Through Trump Ties
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: An August 2025 New York Times report described Binance founder Changpeng Zhao’s campaign for a presidential pardon, including lobbyists and a business deal. The supplied account also links pardons for Zhao, Arthur Hayes and Ross Ulbricht to Trump-family crypto interests. The linked article predates Zhao’s reported October pardon and cannot establish that investments or business ties secured clemency.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: An August 2025 New York Times report described Binance founder Changpeng Zhao’s campaign for a presidential pardon, referring to lobbyists and a business deal. The account also names BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes and Silk Road founder Ross Ulbricht as crypto figures Trump pardoned in 2025, and says Ulbricht’s release fulfilled a campaign promise to Bitcoin advocates. It connects Zhao’s later pardon to Binance’s work on the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial stablecoin. These events raise questions about how presidential clemency intersected with political support and crypto business relationships. But the linked Times article was published before Zhao’s stated October 23 pardon, and its title describes a campaign for clemency rather than proof that a business relationship purchased it. The supplied facts also do not show that investing in Trump-linked ventures provided legal protection or caused any of the pardons. The title asserts that executives bought clemency through Trump ties; that causal claim remains unsupported by the linked report. A reliable chronology and evidence connecting a specific pardon decision to a financial benefit are needed to support that conclusion.

prior_terminal_row.description_short: Pilot Logs Document 11 Epstein Flights Involving Trump
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: Flight logs maintained by Jeffrey Epstein's pilot David Rodgers, entered into evidence in federal proceedings, document at least 11 occasions between 1993 and 1998 when Donald Trump flew on aircraft associated with Epstein. The logs show Trump traveling on Epstein's Gulfstream jet to locations including New York, Atlantic City, Palm Beach, and the Virgin Islands. While the logs document Trump's presence, Trump has denied knowledge of Epstein's trafficking activities. Multiple accusers have alleged that Trump-connected social events served as recruitment grounds for Epstein's trafficking network.

The travel described in the packet documents association; by itself it does not establish knowledge of or participation in Epstein’s trafficking. title: Puerto Rico Hurricane Maria Response — Paper Towels, 3,000 Deaths, Delayed FEMA

prior_terminal_row.title: Puerto Rico Hurricane Maria Response — Paper Towels, 3,000 Deaths, Delayed FEMA
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Puerto Rico Hurricane Maria Response — Paper Towels, 3,000 Deaths, Delayed FEMA
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico in September 2017. The federal response drew criticism over delays and supplies, and Donald Trump’s visit included a widely criticized paper-towel distribution scene. Trump later disputed the nearly 3,000-death estimate from a George Washington University study, calling it politically motivated. The event raised questions about disaster response and how officials described the death toll.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, causing widespread destruction and a prolonged emergency for the island’s residents. President Donald Trump visited on October 3, where he tossed rolls of paper towels to people gathered at a distribution center, a scene widely criticized as out of step with the scale of the disaster. The administration’s response also faced criticism over delays in aid and the timing of federal support. A George Washington University study later estimated that nearly 3,000 people died in connection with the hurricane, far above early counts. Trump publicly rejected the estimate and described it as a Democratic conspiracy. The numbers reflected different stages of assessing deaths after a disaster; the later estimate included deaths occurring in the months after landfall. The response also involved disputes over the Jones Act waiver, FEMA deployment and disaster funding, each unfolding on a different timeline. The event remains an example of a natural disaster becoming a dispute over federal relief and official acknowledgement of deaths.

prior_terminal_row.description_short: Trump Calls Journalists 'Scum,' 'Human Garbage,' 'Enemy' at Rallies
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: Throughout his first term, Trump used campaign rallies to direct physical hatred at journalists, calling them 'scum,' 'human garbage,' 'the enemy,' and other dehumanizing epithets while crowds cheered and sometimes turned threateningly toward press pens. Numerous journalists reported being surrounded by hostile crowds, receiving death threats, and facing physical intimidation at Trump events. Several foreign leaders cited Trump's rhetoric to justify their own crackdowns on domestic press.

title: January 6th 'Fight Like Hell' - Inciting Insurrection

prior_terminal_row.title: January 6th 'Fight Like Hell' - Inciting Insurrection
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: On January 6, 2021, Donald Trump addressed supporters as Congress met to count electoral votes, repeating false claims about the 2020 result and urging the crowd to “fight like hell.” A mob breached the Capitol and interrupted the count. Later that day, Trump asked the crowd to leave while saying, “we love you; you’re very special.”
prior_terminal_row.description_long: On January 6, 2021, Donald Trump delivered a speech to thousands of supporters gathered in Washington D.C., repeatedly claiming the 2020 election was 'stolen' and urging them to march to the Capitol to 'fight like hell' or 'you're not going to have a country anymore.' Trump told the crowd 'we're going to walk down to the Capitol' and 'if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore,' while promoting false claims about election fraud that had been rejected by courts, election officials, and his own administration. Following his speech, thousands of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol, breaking windows, assaulting police officers, and forcing lawmakers to flee for their lives as they attempted to certify Joe Biden's electoral victory. Five people died during the attack, including Capitol Police officer Brian Sicknick, and more than 140 police officers were injured. Trump initially resisted calls to tell his supporters to leave, instead tweeting criticism of Vice President Mike Pence while the Capitol was under siege.
